analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to pass insulin discounts directly to patients at the pharmacy counter.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; with the House session over in January 2023, it died without a floor vote, leaving negotiated insulin discounts with the plans and their middlemen.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, drug makers give Medicare plans big discounts on insulin, but those savings often stay inside the insurance plans and their pharmacy benefit managers instead of showing up as lower copays at the pharmacy. This bill would require plans to pass an increasing share of those negotiated insulin discounts straight to the patient at the register — half in 2022, three-quarters in 2023, all of it by 2024 — and would direct the government's watchdog to report each year on whether insulin prices and patient costs actually fell.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use insulin, who would see the rebates their plans negotiate reflected as lower costs at the pharmacy counter instead of buried in plan accounting.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to pass 100% of negotiated price concessions on insulin to beneficiaries at the point of sale by 2024, phasing up from 50% in 2022 and 75% in 2023.
Requires plans to report their aggregate negotiated insulin concessions in their annual bids and adds new disclosure information, so regulators and patients can see whether the discounts reach them.
Directs the Government Accountability Office to study and report annually on insulin list and net prices, patient out-of-pocket savings, and the market entry of cheaper biosimilar insulin.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare Part D insurance plans, which would keep less of the negotiated insulin discounts; plans could recoup this through higher premiums spread across all enrollees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cap insulin list prices, so manufacturers could keep raising the sticker price and erode the value of the concessions being passed through.
It covers only insulin in Medicare Part D, leaving out uninsured patients and people with commercial insurance who face the same pharmacy counter problem.
Forcing the discounts to the pharmacy counter takes money plans currently use to lower premiums for all enrollees, so it could modestly raise Part D premiums for people who do not use insulin.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare insulin users the benefit is real and immediate: cash savings at the counter. The cost is a modest shift in plan finances, potentially showing up as slightly higher premiums for other enrollees, and the bill does nothing about the underlying list prices manufacturers charge. It is a narrow fix rather than a solution, but the fix it offers is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never moved again; the session ended with no markup and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Burgess introduced the bill on February 18, 2022, joined by Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on February 21, 2022.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plans keep the negotiated insulin discounts that the bill would have redirected to patients, and insulin manufacturers face no added pressure on list prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plans

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Insulin Savings for Patients Act.

for.name: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks
for.what_they_did: Joined Burgess in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill was never brought up by the Democratic majority, so the party split on this specific bill is unknown because no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: PBMs negotiate insulin discounts for Medicare plans and keep a share of them; the bill requires that share to reach the patient instead. The bill's whole point is to end this practice for insulin.

Plans would lose the insulin concessions they now bank, though the bill lets plans reflect the concessions in their bids and lets the Secretary adjust the pass-through percentage with justification to enrollees. They could offset losses through premiums.
Cheaper insulin at the counter could raise demand, and the bill does not cap list prices, but annual government reporting on list versus net prices and biosimilar entry adds pricing scrutiny.
